articles.title: MORNING GLORY: Five Senate races show why Democrats may regret their primary choices
articles.summary: GOP's closing pitch: just vote for the normal people. Five Senate races pit mainstream Republicans against Abdul El-Sayed and other radical Democrats.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed. James Talarico. Peggy Flanagan. Troy Jackson. Chris Pappas. These are not your parents’ Democrats. They aren’t even the 2016 or 2020 Democrats. They aren’t even Kamala Harris Democrats. MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS Across five battleground Senate races, Democrats have nominated "outliers" — hard-left radicals whose appeals to voters have sent their would-be constituents headed toward the GOP’s alternatives in each state where the races are being waged. In Michigan, radical Abdul El-Sayed beat Rep. Haley Stevens —an old-school, big-government liberal — by 1 percentage point in a race that pollsters often had him up by double digits, and his smallest projected margin had been seven points. Voters were turning on him even then as they learned more about his radical views. SCANDALS, SOCIALISTS AND TRUMP ROIL PRIMARIES, SEND INCUMBENTS PACKING AT NEAR-RECORD PACE El-Sayed eked out a win in the primary, but mainstream Republican Mike Rogers, who served 14 years in the House of Representatives, including a term as chair of the House Intelligence Committee, quickly established himself as a normal, pro-American Michigander with a love of football, Mackinac Island and Ford trucks — all of which El-Sayed had disparaged. Meanwhile, El-Sayed tried without effect to delete radical Hasan Piker from his bio, even though everyone in Michigan had seen Piker carry El-Sayed over the primary’s finish line and campaign with the self-proclaimed America-hater on the last day of the primary campaign. "Advantage Rogers," especially as early absentee voting begins in Michigan next week. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico insists on driving off independents and moderates from his Senate campaign with wacky statements and positions that just keep coming. This week, a friendly questioner caught Talarico exiting a campaign event stage and asked, "Who is your favorite drag queen?" SHOCK POLL: TALARICO TIES PAXTON IN TEXAS SENATE RACE, THREATENING GOP STRONGHOLD Talarico didn’t miss a beat or take a breath: "Oh, my gosh. Probably Alyssa Edwards." Talarico’s Texas opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, will no doubt be using that clip in ads blanketing the Lone Star State soon. There just are not that many Texans who can quickly name their favorite drag queen as they would a restaurant, a pizza topping or a Dallas Cowboys player. In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins is always an electoral powerhouse and never more so than this year as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee — probably the most coveted seat in the entire Senate for a senator who wants to make sure his or her state’s critical priorities are funded. DEMOCRATS WHO ‘NEVER VOTED REPUBLICAN’ BACK ROGERS OVER EL-SAYED IN RAZOR-CLOSE RACE Voting against Collins in any year would be unusual — she embodies Maine’s moderation on political matters — but this year her seniority and 10,000 consecutive roll call votes have brought her to the top of the Senate’s food chain. She first drew Graham Platner as her challenger, but he had to quit the race after being engulfed in scandals. Democrats then turned to Troy Jackson, a perennial candidate who finished third in this year’s Democratic primary for governor in the Pine Tree State and whose charisma deficit is immense, made more difficult by the unusual features of his personal and political journey. TAFOYA MAKES 'COMMON SENSE' PITCH TO DISAFFECTED DEMOCRATS AS SHE VOWS TO FIGHT MINNESOTA’S ‘SOCIALIST LURCH’ In Minnesota, cresting fraud scandals drove Gov. Tim Walz from the governor’s race, but his partner in failing to pay attention to alleged fraud schemes, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, slipped through a crowded field and brought her DSA-adjacent and Bernie Sanders-endorsed politics to a Senate campaign in which she is matched against "super-normie" Michele Tafoya, the longtime NFL reporter who has earned five Emmys. Tafoya surged to a tie in deep-blue Minnesota because the state is simply weary of progressive indifference to crime and fraud, and Tafoya is the definition of a "smart moderate." Finally, New Hampshire Democrats turned to left-wing political lifer Chris Pappas to run for the seat being left open by the retirement of moderate Democrat Jean Shaheen. Pappas has been running for office since he graduated from Harvard in 2002. With each step up the Democratic organizational chart, he’s gone further to the left. Now he’s finally getting close to the Senate (and no doubt sees himself in the White House in a few years), only to run into a massive roadblock: John Sununu. NEW HAMPSHIRE CANDIDATE JOHN SUNUNU BLASTS DEMS FOR NOVING ‘FIRST IN THE NATION PRIMARY’ ON RUTHLESS The Sununu family has been serving New Hampshire voters in every sort of way for decades. They are all MIT engineers, and they are all moderates. Their political brand is among the best in America, and John Sununu’s decision to leave the success he has achieved in the private sector to serve Granite State citizens again is a sharp contrast to the forever-in-government Pappas. With moderate New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte also up for re-election, Sununu has the wind at his back and is running the classic New Hampshire retail campaign, where voters expect to see their Senate candidates everywhere. NEWT GINGRICH: REPUBLICANS CAN WIN THE 2026 MIDTERMS — IF THEY FOLLOW THE PLAN There are four other competitive Senate races of note: in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina. All four states were carried by President Trump in 2024, so every Republican has a good shot, especially incumbent Ohio Sen. John Husted, who is running against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who had been in office for five decades until Buckeye voters finally tossed him out two years ago as too liberal for Ohio. All four will be hard-fought through the close of polls on November 3, but the five described above, in which Democrats nominated radicals and ultra-progressives? Not so much. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In the Tea Party years, the GOP fell into the trap of nominating candidates who made moderates in both parties and independents shake their heads, and Democrats won again and again. Now the left has seized control of the Democratic Party, at least for a season, and Republicans are benefiting from the lack of discipline in the Democratic primaries. This is how America always self-corrects against political excess. When El-Sayed, Talarico and others get rejected in November, Democrats will have a chance to reset "between the 40s" of American politics. It’s time for voters to send the Democrats a loud message, just as they did years ago to Republicans: Nominate normal people, or lose, lose, lose. articles.title: In 2004, a meteorite crashed through an Auckland roof and struck a sofa; the family rejected NZ$50,000 before a museum bought the space rock for NZ$40,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2004, a meteorite crashed through an Auckland home, landing on a sofa. The family turned down a NZ$50,000 offer before selling it to the Auckland Museum for NZ$40,000. Read the fascinating story of this rare celestial object and its unique journey.
articles.body: A quiet Saturday morning in Auckland took an extraordinary turn in June 2004 when a piece of rock from space punched through the roof of a suburban home. The meteorite struck the living room of Brenda and Phil Archer's house in Ellerslie, bounced off a leather sofa and hit the ceiling before coming to rest on the floor. Nobody was injured, but the impact left a hole in the roof and a family suddenly in possession of one of New Zealand's rarest natural objects. According to the New Zealand Herald, the Archers received a NZ$50,000 offer for the meteorite but chose not to sell it to an overseas buyer, preferring to keep the rock in New Zealand. The meteorite was eventually acquired by Auckland Museum for NZ$40,000.The morning a rock came through the roofThe meteorite fell around 9.30 am on 12 June 2004. At that time, Brenda Archer was inside the house when she witnessed an enormous explosion. The room was full of dust, and they did not know what to do in the moment. According to the Meteoritical Bulletin, the recovered stone had a mass of about 1.3 kilograms and was officially recorded as the Auckland meteorite. It was classified in the database as an L5 ordinary chondrite and became the ninth meteorite recovered in New Zealand. The official record also identified the Archer family home in Ellerslie as its fall location and recorded the time as 9.30 am.The circumstances of the fall made the specimen unique, as meteorites did not often make it to Earth, and an even rarer occurrence was that of recovering the meteorite immediately upon hitting the ground. This meteorite did not fall into an empty field where it would be found only years later by chance; it declared itself with a crash through a family's roof.From living-room wreckage to scientific specimenThe stone was initially described in news reports as roughly grapefruit-sized and around four billion years old. Scientists at the University of Auckland examined it soon after the fall, confirming that it was extraterrestrial material. Its value was not simply because it had come from space, but because the circumstances of its arrival provided a well-documented example of a meteorite fall.More detailed scientific work came much later. Research published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science examined fragments supplied by Auckland Museum and used mineral chemistry, electron microscopy and oxygen-isotope measurements to investigate the stone's history. The researchers classified it as an L5 ordinary chondrite that had experienced severe shock metamorphism, while also finding that its fusion crust had been chemically altered as the meteorite passed through Earth's atmosphere. This research provided more details about the state in which the meteorite arrived in Auckland. The inside of the rock was well preserved, while the outside had been heated and melted as it entered Earth's atmosphere. Researchers found that oxygen from the atmosphere was incorporated into the fusion crust.The offer the family refusedThe scientific identification quickly turned the meteorite into a collector's item. Offers arrived from overseas, including one reported offer of NZ$50,000. The Archers rejected it. They said they wanted the meteorite to remain in New Zealand and to be displayed publicly rather than disappear into a private collection. That decision eventually led to the Auckland War Memorial Museum acquiring the stone for NZ$40,000. The museum displayed it from July 2004, and the meteorite was subsequently included in exhibitions elsewhere in New Zealand.The Auckland meteorite, apart from its scientific significance, is known today due to the unique manner in which it was discovered. New Zealand had documented only a few meteorites before this fall, which was unusual because it landed on an inhabited house. The meteorite created an unusual collision between everyday life and astronomy. One moment the Archers were having a normal Saturday at home; the next, a rock from an ancient asteroid had crashed through their roof and onto their couch. The damaged house was repaired. The sofa was replaced. But the 1.3-kilogram stone was rare: a piece of the Solar System with a documented path from space to suburban Auckland. The end result was its placement in a museum, making sure that the spectacular event was part of the country’s scientific legacy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1980, one man bought a Quebec island to help eider ducks; 24 years later, it became the region’s first private nature reserve
articles.summary: US News: Discover the inspiring story of Gaston Déry and his 40-year commitment to restoring Île aux Pommes, transforming it into Quebec's first private nature reserve that protects eider ducks and their habitat.
articles.body: Some conservation stories begin with a large government project; others begin quietly with one person deciding a piece of land is worth conserving. The narrative of a small island in the estuary of the St Lawrence River in Quebec is very much of the second kind, and it took the better part of four decades for its entire significance to become obvious.Île aux Pommes is a small island in the middle estuary of the St. Lawrence River, near Saint-Éloi in Quebec's Bas-Saint-Laurent region. The protected reserve covers about 23.53 hectares and includes the main island along with nearby islets and tidal flats. The island had been a popular summer getaway and breeding site for the region’s common eider ducks for many years and was held by the Déry family since Gaston Déry’s grandfather bought it in 1927. By the 1950s, the ecological balance had shifted. Tens of thousands of gulls and several thousand cormorants occupied the island, their droppings degrading the vegetation while gulls preyed on eider eggs and ducklings.Buy the problem to remedy itIn November 1980, Gaston Déry, 28, bought the island from his father with one clear intention. He was a trained forestry engineer and had spent the last two summers looking at the damage close-up. He thought the degradation could be reversed if someone was willing to put in the work. Déry had visited repeatedly in 1979 and 1980. According to the Société de protection et d'aménagement de l'Île aux Pommes, Déry's repeated visits during the summers of 1979 and 1980 allowed him to assess the damage and develop a plan to restore suitable habitat for eider ducks.What followed was slow, hands-on work, not dramatic work. Déry worked with Ducks Unlimited Canada and the Canadian Wildlife Service to set controlled burns to get rid of the heavily degraded vegetation affected by decades of seabird guano, then brought in dirt to cover the empty depressions left behind. In their place were planted shrubs designed for the harsh coastal climate, providing the female eiders with the low dense cover they require to hide their eggs from predators. None of it was an overnight success, and Déry has said the endeavour very much took the next 40 years of his life.An island slowly came back to its birdsThe perseverance paid off not instantly but slowly. As the restored shrubland matured, the number of eider ducks on Île aux Pommes grew year after year, reaching over 3,000 nesting pairs by 2019, a remarkable recovery for an island where nesting habitat had become severely degraded. As the flora on the island stabilised, a greater variety of seabirds, including eiders, returned, transforming a severely degraded habitat into a productive nesting area.Déry supported the comeback with rules that went way beyond simple habitat repair. Pesticides and non-native plant species are banned outright, rainwater on the island is collected and utilised sparingly and the family home itself is run on solar power. In 2004, Quebec formally recognized the Île-aux-Pommes reserve as a private protected area in perpetuity. The announcement by the Quebec Ministry of Environment listed the newly designated conservation sites, including Île aux Pommes, which was declared the very first privately owned nature reserve in the maritime estuary of the St Lawrence and given permanent legal protection under the province’s Natural Heritage Conservation Act.Recognition that stretched much beyond the islandBecause Île aux Pommes remains closed to the general public for the sake of the nesting birds, most people will only ever see it through the work of the researchers and journalists who occasionally grant access, including biologists studying the estuary’s eider colonies and camera crews from Radio Canada’s long-running series La Semaine Verte. Déry's conservation work was formally recognised in 2018, when he was appointed to the Order of Canada for his contributions to the biodiversity and protection of the St. Lawrence estuary, including the revitalisation and conservation of Île aux Pommes.Today, the island of Île aux Pommes is owned by Déry’s two children, who have continued the restoration work that their father began when he was a young man, confident that sustained restoration work could help rebuild the island’s habitats. What started in 1980 as a private effort to restore eider habitat turned into a permanently protected reserve in 2004.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Kempton Park killings: Ninth woman's body found in South Africa's Dawn Park
articles.summary: South Africa police have cautioned against assuming that all the killings are linked but many women are afraid.
articles.body:
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months, amid growing concern over a string of unexplained deaths east of Johannesburg.

The latest victim was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Dawn Park on Thursday morning, police said. Her identity has not yet been released.

The discovery follows the deaths of eight other women whose bodies have been found since July across Ekurhuleni, a major urban area of Johannesburg.

Several of the women were found partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds

President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings , which he said were "causing fear and uncertainty in our communities".

Among the victims was 38-year-old Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo, who disappeared last week after leaving her home for an afternoon run. Her body was found three days later behind a hotel in Kempton Park.

Two other victims have since been identified as Itumeleng Kekana, who had been missing since July, and 38-year-old Dineo Evelyn Motapane, whose body was discovered by the roadside in KwaThema on Tuesday.

The first of the nine bodies was discovered in Kempton Park on 15 July. A suspect was arrested two days later in connection with that case and remains in custody, but police have not linked that suspect to the other deaths.

Further bodies were discovered in August and September, including in Kempton Park, Olifantsfontein, Clayville and KwaThema.

The latest body is of a woman believed to be in her 30s and appeared to have bruises and stab wounds, local media reported.

The discovery has sparked fear in the area, particularly among women who say they no longer feel safe.

"We are scared to come out of our houses. We are scared to go to the shops. We are no longer free in a country where we are supposed to be safe as women," local resident Bongeka Sebela told the BBC.

Police have assembled a multidisciplinary team of detectives, intelligence officers, forensic experts and other specialists to investigate the deaths and establish whether there are links between the cases.

They are also pursuing a person of interest, although they have not disclosed which case or cases that person may be connected to.

"Let's not get emotional, the gloves are off," said Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi on Thursday, adding that the authorities had the capacity to deal with the killings.

In a statement on Thursday, South African police said the recent rise in serious and violent crimes against women remained a "matter of grave concern", urging women in the country to remain vigilant about their personal safety.

They advised women to avoid walking alone or using isolated routes, remain alert to strangers and suspicious vehicles, and share their location or travel plans with someone they trust. They also advised against walking with earphones or earbuds at high volume, warning this could reduce awareness of their surroundings.

"Practising personal safety measures can save lives."

Authorities have offered a 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) reward for information that could lead to arrests and have appealed to families with missing relatives to help identify the remaining victims.

The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concern about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.

Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.

Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has cautioned against speculation, saying investigators were dealing with what appeared, at this stage, to be "quite distinct, separate events".

South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.

Last November, the country classified violence against women a national disaster following an online campaign that culminated in countrywide protests.

articles.title: Wolves and Albion issue warning over derby disorder
articles.summary: The clubs issue a statement ahead of Sunday's meeting after trouble flared when the teams last met.
articles.body:
Wolves and West Bromwich Albion have stressed ahead of their first league meeting in five years that there will be serious consequences for supporters who engage in violence and disorder.

In a joint statement issued before Sunday's Championship match at Molineux, they said trouble at an FA Cup meeting between the clubs in 2024 saw 43 people arrested, 12 charged and sentenced and five given permanent club bans.

Play at The Hawthorns two years ago was halted for 38 minutes after police were assaulted, missiles were thrown and flares were set off.

Wolves and Albion said supporters could "expect enhanced stewarding, policing, robust ticketing controls and additional safety measures" on Sunday.

The clubs stated on Thursday that outcomes following 2024's cup match demonstrated "disorder, violence and criminal behaviour carry significant consequences and will continue to be dealt with robustly" by them and police.

Wolves won the tie two years ago in what was the first match between the clubs in front of fans since 2012.

The clubs said they had worked "closely with the Safety Advisory Group, local authorities and police to ensure appropriate arrangements" were in place for Sunday's Championship game, which kicks off at 12:00 BST.

Fans were "reminded that anyone found engaging in violence, discriminatory behaviour, entering the pitch or trackside areas, throwing missiles, using pyrotechnics or breaching ground regulations risks arrest, prosecution, football banning orders and long-term or permanent exclusion from their club".

The two clubs asked supporters to only use tickets bought through official channels and to sit in the correct designated home or away area.

"Anyone found attempting to access, or being in an incorrect area, will be refused entry or ejected and may face further sanction," they added.

The clubs also asked fans to arrive in good time to allow for security searches and stadium entry procedures, follow instructions of stewards and police and report any unsafe, discriminatory or anti-social behaviour.

They said: "The overwhelming majority of Albion and Wolverhampton Wanderers supporters attend this fixture to support their team passionately and responsibly, and we are confident that will once again be the case."

articles.title: Alton Towers to introduce virtual queuing for disabled riders
articles.summary: The Merlin pass, to be also in use at Legoland and Thorpe Park, is to be launched at Alton Towers.
articles.body:
A new virtual queuing system for visitors with accessibility needs to be introduced first at Alton Towers has been praised by charities.

The upgraded ride access pass (Rap), to be in use later at other Merlin-run parks like Thorpe Park and Legoland Windsor Resort, enables queuing for rides via an app rather than in physical lines.

The news follows a backlash in February when proposed changes led to visitors with conditions such as ADHD and autism being told they would not be able to use a physical Rap .

There will be no change to the eligibility criteria for the pass, available to those who have problems queuing for long periods because of a physical, emotional or learning need, Merlin says.

Staffordshire-based Alton Towers will start accepting the revamped pass at the end of the year, with Merlin's other theme parks taking it on next year.

During the row earlier in the year, families of children with additional needs told the BBC the restrictions would mean their children could not visit because of waiting in long queues, or sensory overload felt in crowded environments.

Under the plan, visitors to places like Alton Towers, Chessington World of Adventures and Legoland Windsor over half-term who had "difficulty with crowds" would no longer have qualified.

Merlin backtracked on the proposal days later following an online petition against it signed by more than 25,000, saying they had listened to the feedback and would pause the changes while considering other options.

However, disability experts, charities and partners such as Disability Rights UK, Scope, ADHD UK, and the National Autistic Society have welcomed the new virtual system, which they helped to shape.

Lisa Myers, of the National Autistic Society, said she was pleased Merlin had consulted with autistic people and their families and that the Rap eligibility criteria would not change.

"This is an example of an adaptation that can make a real difference to autistic people, enabling them to access facilities and venues," she said.

"We have worked with Merlin for many years so we know how committed the team is to ensuring their facilities are welcoming and inclusive for autistic visitors."

John McLachlan, interim chief executive of disability charity Scope, said the new system represented "a positive step in removing unnecessary barriers, to improve the experience of disabled visitors".

Currently Merlin-run parks operate a reverse queue system for Rap holders, meaning they must pre-book a slot in advance to skip the queue for a ride, then wait before they can go on another.

Under the new system, pass holders will wait for the same amount of time as those in physical queues and be notified on the app when they are near the front, meaning they can pass the time where they are most comfortable.

Pass holders will then be helped to join a separate queue using a dedicated entrance.

Merlin's chief operating officer, Rob Smith, said the firm had "listened carefully" to feedback from Rap users, charities and partners and believed the new system would "significantly improve visits".

"It's clear the current experience does not always provide the flexibility and comfort some guests need," he said.

"This new virtual queuing approach has been designed in response to that feedback."

He added the firm wanted every guest to enjoy "memorable days out" and would continue to work closely with Rap users and advocacy group as the new system was rolled out.

articles.title: Trump claims direct talks with Iran: Is diplomacy picking up again?
articles.summary: The US president says Washington is ‘hopefully toward the end’ of Iran war, as global energy prices remain high.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump says the United States is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran, claiming that he has directly spoken to officials in Tehran, raising the prospect of renewed diplomacy even as fighting has erupted in Yemen.

However, there is still no confirmation from Tehran that direct negotiations with Washington have resumed. Just a day earlier, a senior Iranian official publicly rejected talks unless Iran’s conditions were met. Tehran, which has, in effect, closed the Strait of Hormuz, has been demanding that the US honour the terms of the deal signed in June.

Trump’s comments come as the conflict has expanded into Yemen, putting increasing pressure on global energy supplies amid an Iran-imposed blockade of the strait through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes. Oil prices crossed $100 per barrel last week and continue to rise as Iran-linked Houthis have damaged Saudi oil installations amid renewed fighting.

So, what is the latest on the diplomatic front, and will the war end soon?

“Well, hopefully we are toward the end of the war,” he told reporters on Wednesday. “They want to make a deal. We’ll see how that works out.”

When asked by a reporter whether he had recently heard from the Iranian side, Trump said he had spoken with them “directly”.

The comments come after Trump on Monday said he was open to talks, and added that Iran “wants to make a deal, quickly and badly” and that he would decide whether Washington would engage with Tehran.

However, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, accused Trump of sending “mixed signals” and said “no talks until Iran’s conditions are met”.

Trump’s claim that he has heard from Iran “directly” is significant because negotiations between Washington and Tehran have repeatedly depended on intermediaries, including Qatar, Pakistan and Oman. This is not the first time that Trump has claimed direct communication with Iran.

Former Iranian diplomat Abbas Khameyar dismissed Trump’s claims. “I don’t think there has been any additional effort beyond what was already under way in recent weeks,” he told Al Jazeera.

There is a US narrative, he stated, “with tweets and statements by President Trump claiming that the Iranians are calling, pleading and asking for a meeting. But nobody believes this, and matters have not unfolded in that way.”

He added that Iran’s diplomatic activity has not moved beyond the framework already in place in recent weeks, centred on securing enforcement of the existing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) rather than opening new negotiations.

What is the latest on the US-Iran diplomacy front?

On Thursday, Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held a telephone call with Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who has been leading the high-stakes diplomatic and mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran.

Araghchi held the phone call while still in Beijing, during which they discussed and consulted on the latest regional developments and issues of mutual interest, according to Tasnim.

A day earlier, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi called on the US and Iran to exercise restraint and “reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date”, following his meeting with Araghchi in Beijing.

Araghchi, in a statement after the meeting, said that Tehran seeks “the restoration of calm to the region and friendly and peaceful relations with our neighbours”.

“In this regard we have begun dialogue with the countries of the region,” he added.

In a post on X, Araghchi described consultations with Chinese officials as “successful”, saying Tehran values the strategic partnership it has built with Beijing.

“Today’s decisions will decide the future strategic balance in the region, with immeasurable knock-on effects,” Araghchi said on Thursday.

China has avoided direct involvement in the war, but President Xi Jinping, at the BRICS summit in New Delhi over the weekend, offered Beijing’s willingness to play a role in peace efforts. He called on BRICS nations to advance peace in the Middle East.

Huiyao Wang, president of the Center For China and Globalization think tank in Beijing, says China’s role in international affairs is increasing in importance during the current geopolitical turmoil.

“China has an enormous role to exercise if needed. So the mere fact that the two fighting parties have no end in sight shows the need for a big guarantor to come in … I think the US wants to end this war and they also need China’s help,” Wang told Al Jazeera.

Meanwhile, US media outlet Axios is reporting that Trump is expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly next week to discuss the conflict, which has hugely affected oil exports from the Middle Eastern countries.

Diplomatic efforts have repeatedly stalled since a Pakistan-brokered MoU signed by Washington and Tehran collapsed last month, as the two sides accused each other of violating their commitments.

The MoU was supposed to kick-start a 60-day period for peace talks between the warring sides and included provisions for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a major flashpoint in the war.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier this month that Tehran would return to the agreement if Washington did the same.

What do we know about the Houthi meeting with US officials?

US officials met representatives of Yemen’s Houthi movement at the US embassy in Muscat over the weekend, five sources told Reuters news agency. Oman helped organise the meeting.

The Houthis told US officials they did not intend to attack American vessels and remained committed to their 2025 ceasefire with Washington, according to two sources.

One source said they also pledged not to target Israeli or other commercial vessels, with the exception of Saudi ships.

The conflict had largely subsided in recent years after a 2022 ceasefire between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis, but reignited in July.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline to cement their grip on the key Bab al-Mandeb strait – a vital maritime route connecting Asia with Europe – while declaring a blockade on Saudi shipping.

The strategic waterway is a critical maritime corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has become an alternative shipping route as the US war against Iran choked the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Homebuyers stay resilient as rising prices push demand towards premium homes
articles.summary: News News: Homebuyers in India remain inclined towards real estate despite concerns over rising property prices, with preferences shifting towards larger homes, .
articles.body: Homebuyers in India remain inclined towards real estate despite concerns over rising property prices, with preferences shifting towards larger homes, higher budgets and newly launched projects. The trend suggests that buyers are adapting to higher prices rather than stepping away from the housing market.According to Anarock’s latest consumer sentiment survey, 60 percent of 8,320 respondents across 14 cities preferred real estate as an investment asset during January to June 2026. Stock markets were preferred by 20 percent, gold by 11 percent and fixed deposits by 9 percent.Bigger homes gain preferenceThe survey found that 48 percent of respondents preferred 3BHK homes, while 38 percent preferred 2BHK units. Preference for 4BHK and larger homes stood at 5 percent.The preference for 3BHK homes crossed 50 percent in Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Chennai and Delhi-NCR, while Bengaluru recorded the highest preference for 4BHK-plus homes at 10 percent, Anarock said.The shift towards larger homes is also reflected in buyer budgets. The Rs 90 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore segment was the most preferred budget category, accounting for 34 percent of respondents. At the same time, the share of buyers preferring homes priced below Rs 45 lakh fell to 18 percent from 28 percent in H1 2022.Rising prices remain a concernDespite continued demand, affordability is emerging as a major challenge. Anarock found that 65 percent of respondents were at least moderately concerned about rising housing prices, including 35 percent who were very or extremely concerned.Still, 44 percent said they would proceed with their purchase as planned, while 38 percent said they could delay their decision slightly. Only 18 percent indicated that they could postpone indefinitely or cancel their purchase.Among those considering a delay or cancellation, affordability was the biggest concern, cited by 44 percent. Another 32 percent said fewer properties were available within their budget.New launches attract buyersNewly launched projects are gaining preference over ready-to-move-in homes. Anarock found that 34 percent of respondents preferred new launches, compared with 18 percent who preferred ready-to-move-in properties.Developer reputation and project location were cited by 34 percent of respondents as important factors, while infrastructure development was cited by 22 percent.End-use remained the primary reason for buying, with 68 percent of respondents purchasing mainly for self-use. However, buyers are also considering the investment potential of their homes. Anarock said 67 percent considered resale value important or very important, while 77 percent considered rental income potential important or very important.Anarock’s Q1 2026 residential market data separately showed average housing prices across the top seven cities rising about 7 percent year-on-year, while homes priced above Rs 1.5 crore accounted for 53 percent of new launches during the quarter.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: President John Quincy Adams knew one book people needed to read to become good citizens
articles.summary: John Quincy Adams wrote letters urging his son to read the Bible daily, believing Scripture was essential to raising citizens worthy of the Constitution.
articles.body: Too few American students know enough about our Constitution. Still, fewer know there is such a thing as "Constitution Day." But this year, it might be worth taking up an assignment our sixth president gave to his son in a remarkable series of letters written while President John Quincy Adams served as minister to Russia. Adams did not focus on career advice for his son. He did not teach his son how to make money. Instead, Adams insisted upon this: Read the Bible. Every day. BILL BENNETT: WHAT I TOLD MY SONS ABOUT THEIR FAITH, FAMILY AND AMERICA Adams believed no education could be complete without it. He wrote to his son that when "duly read and meditated on," the Bible is "of all books in the world, that which contributes most to make men good, wise, and happy." And here’s where our Constitution comes in: Adams believed children formed by Scripture would become "useful citizens to their country" and "respectable members of society." GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK There’s much ado today about civics education. And that’s a good thing. More educators and parents should ask: Should students memorize the Constitution? Learn about the three branches of government? Study the Federalist Papers? All extremely important. But John Quincy Adams understood something too many have largely forgotten. AMERICA’S NEXT 250 YEARS DEPEND ON PASSING FAITH AND FREEDOM TO OUR CHILDREN The Constitution details how we, a free people, govern ourselves. But it cannot teach rising generations how to become worthy of that freedom. That is why Adams spent letter after letter introducing his son to the New Testament and to the Hebrew Bible — to Genesis, Exodus, the Ten Commandments, and to the Law of Moses. He argued the Mosaic Law represented the greatest moral revolution of the ancient world because it united justice with humanity. TEN COMMANDMENTS BELONG IN TEXAS SCHOOLS AND THE SUPREME COURT CAN PROTECT THEM Unlike the legal systems of Greece and Rome, which largely emphasized civic order or individual virtue, Adams believed the Hebrew Scriptures taught something unprecedented: Duties toward other people were also duties toward God. The laws protecting the stranger, the widow, the orphan and even enemies reflect a moral vision unlike anything the secular world had produced. Adams admired the Hebrew Bible because it did something no human legislature could accomplish. THE BEDROCK OF AMERICAN LIBERTY WAS LAID IN JERUSALEM It recognized individual merit and responsibility. It legislated for human nature. The Constitution details how we, a free people, govern ourselves. But it cannot teach rising generations how to become worthy of that freedom. Governments can punish theft. They cannot eliminate envy. Governments can outlaw murder. They cannot command honor, gratitude, humility or self-control. John Quincy Adams’s letters were never simply about raising his own successful children. They were about transmitting civilization itself to all America’s children. Too many fathers today have outsourced the most important conversations about duty, morality and character to schools, to government institutions, to coaches or even to celebrities. Mothers play an indispensable role in raising virtuous children, but there is no substitute for the unique influence of an engaged father who teaches his son what it means to be an honorable man. DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE The consequences of absence are all around us. Young Americans increasingly struggle to distinguish rights from responsibilities. They know how to demand respect but not always how to earn it. They have been taught self-esteem more often than self-government. They build professional résumés but little aptitude for disappointment, mental resilience or for duty. ALEX BERENSON: GENTLE PARENTING CAN'T REPLACE THE STRENGTH OF A GOOD DAD This isn't merely an educational, civic or cultural problem. It's a fatherhood problem. For centuries, American fathers understood that one of their highest callings was to introduce their children to the moral inheritance that made liberty possible. Not because government required it. Because freedom required it. The Hebrew Bible teaches children that human beings are capable of both good and evil. Actions have consequences. Morality matters. And it importantly teaches every person bears the image of God. The Founders knew constitutions cannot preserve themselves. Republics depend upon citizens capable of governing themselves before they presume to govern others. John Quincy Adams understood this better than most. His letters to his son were, in many ways, one manual for raising a free citizen. Perhaps that is the lesson we most need today: If we want stronger schools, we need stronger families. If we want better citizens, we need fathers who teach virtues. John Quincy Adams’s letters were never simply about raising his own successful children. They were about transmitting civilization itself to all America’s children. If we want to renew American civics, we should certainly continue teaching the Constitution. articles.title: Common kitchen staple may help relieve mild constipation, new research suggests
articles.summary: Researchers in Japan found that a daily vinegar drink with 750mg of acetic acid led to about 1.2 more bowel movements per week, according to a new study, even as experts urge caution.
articles.body: People who suffer from mild constipation may find some relief with a simple daily vinegar drink, new research suggests, even as experts urge more study and share cautions. Constipation is a condition in which a person generally has fewer than three bowel movements a week, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Stools may also be hard, dry or lumpy and difficult or painful to pass. The NIH says adults should get 22 to 34 grams of fiber a day, depending on age and sex — though fewer than 10% of women and about 3% of men reach the recommended daily intake, according to federal dietary guidelines. THE 8 HEALTHIEST BEANS YOU SHOULD BE EATING MORE OFTEN, ACCORDING TO NUTRITION EXPERT Left untreated, chronic constipation can lead to hemorrhoids and anal fissures and, in severe cases, complications such as fecal impaction that may require emergency care. The NIH recommends changes to diet and lifestyle, such as increasing fiber intake with foods including legumes, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds, as a first step in treating constipation — along with over-the-counter medicines if needed. Now, a new study has found that consuming vinegar in liquid form may also increase bowel movements. Published online in the journal Scientific Reports by Japanese researchers, the study reported that eating vinegar-based dishes more often was positively associated with better defecation status, though it remained unclear how much vinegar and its potentially active ingredient, acetic acid, were necessary to be effective. "Given that acetic acid may play a key role in the effects of vinegar and that its intake can be strictly controlled, we conducted a randomized controlled trial in which healthy adults with mild constipation (defecation frequency of 3–5 times per week) consumed a vinegar beverage instead of vinegar-based dishes to investigate the effects of vinegar on defecation," the researchers wrote. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The researchers randomly assigned a total of 44 participants — healthy Japanese adults between 20 and 69 years old — to consume either a beverage made with vinegar or a placebo drink at breakfast for four weeks. The participants reported to have an average of three to five bowel movements a week, which the researchers classified as mild constipation. The vinegar drink was made by mixing brewed vinegar with water, providing 750 milligrams of acetic acid in each 200-milliliter serving. The placebo used a small amount of citric acid instead of vinegar to give it a similar tart taste, so participants couldn't tell which drink they had. Both drinks were sweetened with sucralose and flavored with apple. "These findings … [support] a potential dietary approach for maintaining bowel health." During the first week, the vinegar group showed trends toward improvement in bowel-movement frequency, number of defecation days and stool volume compared with the placebo group. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ By week four, defecation frequency was "significantly higher" in the vinegar group than in the placebo group — about 1.2 more bowel movements a week — the study concluded. "These findings suggest that daily consumption of vinegar beverages may improve defecation status in healthy adults with mild constipation, supporting a potential dietary approach for maintaining bowel health," the researchers wrote. Both groups experienced gradual improvement over the course of the study — and the researchers suggested that some participants may have been habitually underhydrated, so the added daily drink may have played a part in relieving their constipation. "They did not study typical apple cider vinegar supplements or concentrated vinegar shots." They noted, however, that during the first week, participants in the vinegar group showed signs of greater improvement than those in the placebo group, implying that vinegar or acetic acid may have had an additional early benefit. Limitations of the study The study is intriguing and "a promising clue rather than proof that vinegar treats constipation," Florida-based registered dietitian Jamie Lee McIntyre, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "I wouldn’t leap from this study to recommending apple cider vinegar shots for constipation," she said. "The researchers used a standardized vinegar beverage containing a specific amount of acetic acid. They did not study typical apple cider vinegar supplements or concentrated vinegar shots." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Mizkan Holdings Co. Ltd., a Japanese food company that manufactures vinegar, funded the study; three of the researchers were employed by Mizkan. The scientists further noted that their findings "should be regarded as preliminary and require more confirmation in further studies." "For now, I'd stick with the constipation strategies we know have a stronger evidence base: adequate fiber and fluids, regular physical activity and a consistent bathroom routine," McIntyre said. "Vinegar can certainly be part of a meal, or serve as a wonderful base to a dressing or sauce, but I wouldn't consider it a constipation treatment based on this one small study." Dr. Eric Shah, a gastroenterologist and clinical associate professor at the University of Michigan, told Fox News Digital that there "is this misnomer that drinking more water helps constipation, when it just makes most people have to urinate more." "I wouldn't consider it a constipation treatment based on this one small study." The key to avoiding constipation is to stay adequately hydrated, take soluble fiber and consider pelvic floor physical therapy when needed, which is a growing field that is readily accessible from primary care, he said. "What generally comes out of those water trials is that mineral-rich water, particularly magnesium-rich, tends to help more with constipation in clinical trials. The mineral content is probably more important than the volume of intake for most people." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP McIntyre added that "more vinegar isn't necessarily better." "Because vinegar is highly acidic, drinking it regularly — particularly undiluted — can irritate the esophagus and contribute to dental enamel erosion," she said.

articles.title: Nicholas Brandram's family say he was not 'Putney pusher'
articles.summary: The family of Nicholas Brandram said there was no forensic evidence linking him to the incident.
articles.body:
The family of Nicholas Brandram have insisted he was not the so-called "Putney pusher" and have blamed the Metropolitan Police for his death.

The 44-year-old was under suspicion of being the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017.

Brandram's family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation" and there was no forensic evidence linking the banker to the incident.

The Met has been asked for comment. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had received a "mandatory referral" from the force.

In a statement, the family said there was "no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage".

"In fact, the evidence proved the opposite."

Brandram was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Met confirmed he had been released under investigation.

The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The force said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".

The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview".

"They searched his home, and the Met Police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting," they said.

"For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence.

"He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation."

They said the police were repeatedly asked to end their investigation and warned about the impact the investigation was having on Brandram's mental health, saying: "Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead."

While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.

On Thursday, an IOPC spokesperson said: "We have received a mandatory referral from the Met Police relating to prior contact officers had with Nicholas Brandram, who was sadly found unresponsive and declared deceased on 15 September.

"We are currently assessing the referral before deciding whether further action is required from us."

Shortly after the Putney Bridge incident on 5 May 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."

Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head.

"It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me."

It was reported at the time that around 15 minutes after the push, the jogger came back the other way across the bridge and ignored the victim when she tried to speak to him.

Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident.

The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.

That’s the America I’ll always fight for.”The latest exchange came days after Krishnamoorthi criticised a Department of Homeland Security social media post featuring a man identified as “Mr. Singh”. The DHS post, styled as a movie poster, told “Mr. Singh” to “get off our roads” and warned him to “self-deport or find out”.Krishnamoorthi said the post demonised a name shared by more than 160,000 people in the US and said Sikh and South Asian Americans were “as American as anyone”.Krishnamoorthi’s remarks came amid renewed attention on Langevin, who has repeatedly made comments about Indian immigrants and the Indian American community.What did Chandler Langevin say about Indians?Langevin, a Palm Bay City Council member, came under scrutiny in 2025 over social media posts targeting Indian immigrants. He called for the deportation of Indians and later directed several posts at Krishnamoorthi after the congressman criticised his remarks.In one post, Langevin described Krishnamoorthi as a “foreign occupier” and mocked his name, while referring to his country of origin as “Tatooine”, the fictional planet from the Star Wars franchise.Krishnamoorthi responded that he was born in India, raised in Illinois and elected by voters there.The Palm Bay City Council took action against Langevin in October 2025. On October 2, the council voted 4-1 to ask Florida Governor Ron DeSantis to suspend him from office.Later that month, it voted 3-2 to censure him. The restrictions included limiting his ability to introduce agenda items, speak during council reports and serve on city-appointed boards and committees.Langevin subsequently sued the city, arguing that his First Amendment rights had been violated.The case was settled in February 2026, with Palm Bay agreeing to a USD 55,000 settlement. articles.title: Eurovision: Ireland boycotts contest for second year in a row
articles.summary: In a statement, RTÉ said it feels Ireland's participation "cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza".
articles.body:
Irish broadcaster RTÉ will not broadcast or participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest.

It is the second year in a row that the broadcaster has not participated in the competition.

In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the 2026 contest in Vienna , after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part.

In a statement they said: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk."

Last year Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands and Slovenia boycotted the Eurovision Song Contest, after it was decided Israel could compete.

RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory".

Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden.

The 2027 contest will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the Grand Final being held at the Arena Burgas on 15 May. The semi-finals will take place on 11 and 13 May.

Bulgaria earned the right to host the contest after DARA won Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with Bangaranga, the country's first victory in the competition.

It said the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

articles.title: Vacation paradise under attack as officials suspect arsonists may be behind inferno
articles.summary: Positano Mayor Gabriella Guida suspects arson as wildfires erupted simultaneously across Italy's Amalfi Coast, forcing evacuations and terrifying tourists.
articles.body: A raging wildfire along Italy’s famed Amalfi Coast forced precautionary evacuations and left tourists on edge as emergency crews battled flames across the iconic Mediterranean getaway. Firefighters were deployed in both aerial and ground operations to combat the blaze that broke out in scrubland near Amalfi. Efforts to extinguish the fire continued uninterrupted along the coast after the blaze erupted Monday evening, according to Reuters. STUNNING VACATION HOT SPOT TURNS INTO OVERCROWDED NIGHTMARE AS TOURISTS FLOOD STREETS The flames affected areas surrounding Cus Pogerola, Positano, Amalfi, Tovere di Amalfi and nearby coastal zones, local news outlets reported. Fire crews worked through the night to prevent the flames from reaching residential areas, and no injuries or damage to homes were reported. While strong winds initially prevented helicopters from taking part in the response, firefighting aircraft joined the operation by morning. Italy’s national fire service, Vigili del Fuoco, said on X that emergency crews responded to scrubland fires stretching between Positano, Amalfi, Agerola and Vico Equense along the Amalfi Coast and Sorrento Peninsula. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER A total of seven ground teams and three aircraft were deployed as part of the firefighting operation, according to the Turkish news organization Anadolu Agency. As a precaution, some restaurants and facilities in key locations were evacuated as concerns grew among tourists staying in the region, the news outlet reported. Local leaders warned of severe environmental damage and publicly raised suspicions of arson, Italian newspaper Il Mattino said. Positano Mayor Gabriella Guida confirmed that the fire ravaged the woods of Tordigliano on the border between the Amalfi Coast and the Sorrento Peninsula, the newspaper reported. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The flames reached much of the state road — which was closed to ensure safe firefighting operations — and descended toward Positano. It also threatened upper mountain hamlets in the Capo d’Acqua area before Montepertuso, between Positano and Santa Maria del Castello, according to local newspapers. Guida expressed fears that the loss of centuries-old trees would trigger major hydrogeological disruption and landslides once the first rains arrived, Il Mattino reported. She said she believes the cause was likely arson, pointing out that fires breaking out simultaneously across Vico Equense, Agerola, Amalfi and Positano appeared to indicate a coordinated plan, rather than a coincidence, local outlets reported. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Guida acknowledged the economic toll on the destination, noting that travelers were frightened during what was supposed to be a relaxing vacation. She urged anyone with information about the fires to speak up, according to the newspaper. Sorrento Mayor Corrado Fattorusso released an official statement expressing solidarity with the administrations and communities of the Sorrento Peninsula and the Amalfi Coast, according to local news outlet Il Sole 24 Ore. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Describing the fires as an attack on the region's identity, history and environmental heritage, Fattorusso urged authorities to move from words to action by identifying the culprits and establishing concrete land monitoring and prevention measures. As of midweek, fire crews were still working to extinguish the remaining hot spots in areas around the Amalfi Coast and Sorrento Peninsula, according to numerous reports.

articles.title: Swedish PM Ulf Kristersson resigns after election loss
articles.summary: Left-wing opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson look set to form the next government.
articles.body:
Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election.

He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people.

Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament.

Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election.

His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority.

The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend.

In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.

After a prime minister resigns, the Speaker of the Riksdag holds talks with all parties to proposes a candidate for the next leader, which is then voted on by MPs.

"Now it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am herewith requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that work to start immediately," Kristersson's statement read.

In a speech posted on Instagram, Andersson said: "The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country".

The Social Democrats have regularly led Swedish governments since World War Two and have been the country's dominant political force for much of the last century.

Its leader, Andersson, is expected to return to power after four years in opposition, and has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government.

But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes.

After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days.

In his resignation, Kristersson said the opposition faced "complicated" conditions for forming the next government, "because the parties' various statements before election day could pose obstacles".

The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.

The SD were founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s and were shunned for decades by the mainstream.

But the party has rebranded itself since the mid-2000s, culminating in a watershed moment in 2022 when it became Sweden's second-largest party on a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.

They had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm.

But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022.

A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week.

On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day.

articles.title: Thousands of Barclays staff make return-to-office demands
articles.summary: Unite union, which represents 36,000 Barclays staff, calls for a one-off payment to offset increased travel and childcare costs.
articles.body:
Thousands of Barclays staff are demanding concessions from the bank, including a one-off payment, after it said it wants employees to work from the office more often.

Staff who have been expected to work in the office for two days per week should be in the office for at least three days a week from next month, according to the company.

Unite, which represents about 36,000 Barclays staff, is calling for the bank to reverse its decision. The union is also pressing for exemptions to offset increased travel and childcare costs.

Barclays said many employees already work in the office for three or more days, depending on business need.

The bank sent a memo to staff in July outlining its expectations, which include that senior leaders work at least four days per week in the office.

As first reported in the Financial Times , the bank is facing a growing backlash against the proposed rules change.

Unite national officer Rick Coyle said thousands of employees have signed an open letter calling for Barclays to reverse the decision, and the number of signatories "continues to rise".

He added that Barclays is "trying to fix a problem that doesn't exist" in making its working-from-home rules less flexible.

The open letter says workers are delivering "strong financial results and improved customer services" with its current working from home policy.

It adds that thousands of workers have made suggestions, which the union has condensed into a series of demands.

an exemption for commutes longer than 40 minutes or 35 miles

exemptions during Christmas, summer, and school holidays

a maximum one day in the office for carers

flexibility for wrap-around childcare, and childcare vouchers and onsite creches to be explored

Barclays said in a statement that it recognised "the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations".

"Our minimum time in office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business," a spokesperson said.

The bank declined to say how many staff would be affected by the rules change. However, the BBC understands that there are different rules depending on teams, with, for example, investment bankers in the office for five days per week.

The coronavirus pandemic forced many businesses to allow working from home, depending on the nature of the business.

Since then, many organisations have been clawing workers back into the office, despite evidence that hybrid working may be the best fit .

Amazon, Boots and JP Morgan are some of the organisations that brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day after the pandemic.

This week, Ewan Venters, the executive chair of fashion brand Paul Smith, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that working from home "just doesn't work" for young people and urged the government to stay out of decisions over where employees work.

In June, digital bank Revolut said it was shifting away from its "remote-first" policy for new recruits in 2027, but for other employees that policy wouldn't change.

articles.body: At 16, Michigan student Mason Maressa had saved $3,500 from working while attending high school. He could have used the money to buy a car. Instead, he spent it on a vintage Rolex Air-King, a decision that later became the starting point of his watch business.According to Entrepreneur magazine, Maressa was already interested in luxury goods, especially watches. A few days after the watch arrived, he listed it for sale online. He eventually sold it for about $4,000, making roughly $500 in profit.The amount was not enough to change his life, but the sale showed Maressa that there could be an opportunity in a market he already understood and enjoyed. Rather than spending the money he made, he put it into another watch and continued buying and selling.That process gradually became a business. As Maressa bought more watches, he also learned about the pre-owned luxury watch market. Pricing, condition, references, market demand, authentication and customer relationships became part of his work.For the next several years, he continued trading watches while expanding his inventory. What began with one Rolex gradually became a larger operation, and by his late teens, the watch business had become a serious venture.From online sales to a physical storeThe next major step came when Maressa decided to take the business beyond online transactions. In January 2025, Clocked In opened a brick-and-mortar store at 601 S Beacon Blvd, Suite 103, in Grand Haven, Michigan.The store operates by appointment only. It specialises in pre-owned luxury watches, with brands including Rolex, Omega, Tudor and other recognised names in the industry.The store caters to experienced collectors who may already know the reference they want, as well as people buying a luxury watch for the first time.The store also gives customers the chance to sit down, handle different watches and compare them before making a purchase. Its current business model also includes unworn pieces, according to the company's website.Clocked In says its customer base includes collectors and enthusiasts from West Michigan and beyond. articles.title: In 2019, a Miami woman bought a home after a clean title search; five years later, a disputed $55,650 code enforcement lien is blocking its renovation or sale

articles.body: When Angelica Martinez bought her home in Miami's Little Havana neighbourhood in 2019, she did what most buyers do: she hired an attorney, carried out a title search and checked the property's history for any outstanding debts or liens. Everything seemed perfect. Five years after the purchase, Martinez faces the threat of foreclosure over a $55,650 code enforcement lien that the City of Miami says accumulated against her property. The lien has prevented her from renovating or selling the home, and her attorney argues that it should never have existed in the first place."The City of Miami is stopping my client from fixing her own home over a lien that doesn't exist," Ari Pregen, an attorney with The Code Clinic who represents homeowner Angelica Martinez, told CBS News.A Little Havana homeowner says she feels trapped in the home she purchased.City of Miami code inspectors said they observed contractors replacing roof framing, installing a wood fence and constructing a concrete driveway without permits during a proactive inspection in September 2024.Martinez acknowledges hiring the crew to repair her roof. But she and her attorney dispute her responsibility for the fence and driveway work, which became the subject of the city's code enforcement case."It's just a mistake; a very expensive mistake they're making me pay for," Martinez told the outlet.Her attorney argued that city records show the previous owner completed renovations in 2018. Though the permits from that project do not mention the fence or driveway, Google Earth images from February 2019 appear to show both improvements already in place. This was months before Angelica Martinez bought the property. She talks about the whole process of purchasing the property."I got an attorney, did a title search, everything went through review making sure there was no debt or lien on the house to make sure the house was clean for me to purchase. Zero violations existed. My attorneys reviewed the whole history of the house. There was no issue whatsoever," she told the broadcaster.Following the 2024 inspection, she agreed to lower the fence and bring the driveway into compliance. Her attorney also acknowledged that homeowners can be held responsible for correcting such violations, even when they were not the people who originally carried out the work. According to him, the city inspectors signed an affidavit certifying that Martinez had completed the corrections."Everything was reviewed and they told me I was done and I could go ahead living in my house without any issues," Martinez recalled.However, the City of Miami's account differs. According to Miami's Code Enforcement Department, Martinez was found in violation by the Code Enforcement Board at a hearing on 22 January 2025. The board gave her 120 days to comply and ordered a $150 per day fine if the violations remained after the deadline. The city says the permits for the driveway and fence were submitted on 31 July 2025 and finalised on 9 February 2026. The department said no request for additional time was filed before the deadline expired. What happened next was a lien: $150 multiplied by hundreds of days, bringing it to a $55,650 lien.Pregen argues that such a lien should not exist. His team reportedly went through the city's public records and found no record of any lien against the property. "We looked for the lien in three different ways in the city's own public records and there is no lien recorded. It isn't there, and yet they're still trying to use it to freeze her life," he said.Martinez says the dispute has prevented her from renovating the house or putting it up for sale. She remains in a home trapped between conflicting accounts of compliance and penalty calculations. A mitigation hearing is scheduled before the City of Miami Code Enforcement Board on 22 September.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
