articles.title: Michigan Republican lawmaker warns guaranteed income programs do not work, voices opposition to state policy
articles.summary: Michigan Republicans are demanding oversight of Rx Kids, a $300 million cash assistance program they say has become a guaranteed income experiment.
articles.body: Guaranteed income programs do not work and amount to mere "redistributions of wealth," according to Michigan Republican state Rep. Jay DeBoyer, who joined other Republicans in the state Legislature in criticizing the programs, which have gained prominence in recent years. "Absolutely not. When does that stop?" Rep. DeBoyer, R-Clay Township, told Fox News Digital. "When you think about the role of government, the role of government is not to fund people's lives. The role of the government is to provide a conducive environment where you have opportunities for success." DeBoyer, who chairs the state House Oversight Committee, is leading a contingent of Michigan House Republicans demanding rigorous inspection of Rx Kids — a taxpayer-funded initiative billed as the nation's largest prenatal and infant cash assistance program. Lawmakers are raising alarms over how hundreds of millions of public dollars are being spent. DIRECTOR OF 'CASH GIVEAWAY' PROGRAM TAILORED TO NEW MOTHERS GRILLED ON HOW TAXPAYER FUNDING IS USED IN DEBATE The scrutiny boiled over during a June 2 House Oversight Committee hearing, where GOP lawmakers targeted the program’s lack of spending restrictions or income limits. Republican leaders argue the state-funded initiative has evolved into something far different than what was originally presented to the Legislature, accusing Democrats of using hundreds of millions of dollars in public funding to advance a broader guaranteed-income agenda. Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall told Fox News Digital that lawmakers were led to believe they were funding a targeted maternal and prenatal health initiative — not what he characterized as an open-ended social experiment. Under the current design, Rx Kids provides expectant mothers with a lump-sum payment of $1,500 during pregnancy, followed by $500 per month for six or 12 months after birth, depending on the participating community, regardless of household income. GOP lawmakers across the country have raised similar legal, budgetary, and ideological objections to guaranteed basic income (GBI) and direct cash transfer programs. In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Harris County over its Uplift Harris direct-cash pilot, prompting the Texas Supreme Court to block the payments in 2024. Harris County later terminated Uplift Harris and a successor program in June 2025 and moved to reallocate the funds. In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed Republican-backed legislation that would have prohibited local municipalities and counties from enacting GBI initiatives. Meanwhile, Iowa Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds signed House File 2319 into law on May 1, 2024, banning local guaranteed income programs statewide. CALIFORNIA GUARANTEED INCOME ADVOCACY GROUP RECOMMENDS PERMANENT POLICY FUNDED BY 'DEDICATED LOCAL TAXES' The director of Michigan's Rx Kids, Dr. Mona Hanna, told Fox News Digital that the initiative is neither a traditional guaranteed income program nor a universal basic income (UBI) model, pointing to its strict focus on the critical first year of a child's life. DeBoyer directly challenged that distinction, pointing to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) plan. The state document explicitly defines a "guaranteed income program" as a "cash payment provided on a regular basis to members of a community with no strings attached and no work requirement," citing Rx Kids as a primary example. "The truth is this is just about redistribution of wealth," DeBoyer said. "It's a distribution tactic that I would argue is not going to help moms and babies, when that's actually what we should be trying to do." Progressive advocates have pushed back against the Republican offensive. Adriane Brown, senior communications director for the Economic Security Project (ESP) — an advocacy group founded in 2016 to promote direct cash transfers — argued that direct assistance enjoys bipartisan support. "Cash is widely supported across ideological lines, and there’s long been growing momentum and political appetite for guaranteed income," Brown told Fox News Digital. "The majority of the Michigan Legislature supports this pilot," Brown added. "Republican Senator John DaMoose wrote an op-ed in the Detroit Free Press about how Rx Kids is a pro-life policy and ‘fiscally responsible,’ and the program has been expanded in both urban and rural communities throughout Michigan by both Democrat and Republican leaders." GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE Brown emphasized that economic pressures on young families necessitate immediate, flexible relief. "The bottom line is, people are struggling in our economy," Brown said. "It’s more expensive than ever to have a child. In acute moments of vulnerability, people need all the support they can get. It doesn’t make sense to malign cash assistance as a partisan idea when so many communities would benefit from the stability it offers." Meanwhile, the ESP has been pushing for guaranteed income long before affordability became a salient issue. Founded in 2016, ESP launched with more than "100 entrepreneurs, activists, researchers and philanthropists" advocating for direct cash payments. The ESP helped create over 100 guaranteed income pilots across the U.S. The broader campaign for direct payments includes Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, led by former Stockton, California, Mayor Michael Tubbs. Tubbs, who launched one of the nation's early municipal cash experiments, has long argued that federal tax dollars should fund income supplements to help lower-income Americans keep up with rising inflation, rent and groceries, claiming it's a viable policy to tackle affordability. As many guaranteed income advocates would like to make the policy permanent and even push it at the federal level, only Cook County, Illinois has approved such a measure so far. DeBoyer countered that established social safety nets already exist to support low-income families, but said those programs carry strict eligibility standards and oversight mechanisms that Rx Kids lacks. "We have a safety net. We spend literally billions of dollars on social welfare," DeBoyer said. "The difference is, in this particular spending, there are no parameters. There is no means test. Literally a millionaire qualifies for this program. An individual who's not an American citizen qualifies for this program." At the end of the day, we can say that this is about moms and babies, but that creates the potential for massive abuse."

articles.title: US tariffs against Russian oil buyers pass: What it means for China, India
articles.summary: US sanctions aim to weaken Russian oil exports, heavily targeting China and India as Moscow’s largest energy buyers.
articles.body:
United States Congress has passed a bill that gives President Donald Trump sweeping powers to impose sanctions on Russia’s crude exports as well as steep tariffs on buyers of Russian energy, a measure which will impact Moscow’s biggest customers, China and India .

The legislation, passed in the House of Representatives on Wednesday and sent to Trump to sign into law, is the most significant US action against Moscow since the president’s return to the White House.

The “Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026”, named after the late senator who was a staunch supporter of Ukraine up until his death in July, is designed to curtail the economic pipeline that has enabled Russia to fund its war against Ukraine , now in its fifth year.

Major provisions include new sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin as well as on more than 20 top officials and companies that work with the Russian defence industry. It also targets Russia’s “shadow fleet” of oil tankers and the network it uses to evade international sanctions on energy exports.

The bill gives the president authority to impose sanctions by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). Under it, he will be able to apply tariffs of up to 100 percent on exports to the US from the top five purchasers of Russian energy, military equipment or countries facilitating Russian sanctions evasion.

Tariffs of up to 500 percent can also be applied to Russian imports directly into the US. The US imported $3.8bn in goods from Russia in 2025.

China and India are the top two buyers of Russian energy and likely to be hit hardest by the new legislation. China buys about half of Russian crude oil exports, followed by India at 37 percent, according to August data from the think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).

Turkiye and the European Union each import about 5 percent, the report says.

India, one of the world’s largest crude importers and a country whose dependence on foreign oil is expected to grow further in the coming years, is in a tricky position as its attempts to diversify away from Russian energy were disrupted by the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.

Hours after the US Congress approved the bill, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said New Delhi had raised the issue with various US interlocutors in recent months, and had “very clearly articulated” the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market.

“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” it said in a statement. The government will work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the legislation’s implications, it added.

The pressure could be particularly acute for India. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has warned that India’s rising reliance on crude imports has “major implications” for its energy security. Replacing Russian supplies could also mean sourcing more crude from producers farther away, including in the Americas.

Recent experience suggests India has been more responsive to Western pressure over Russian oil purchases than China. According to the IEA, tanker-tracking data show Indian imports of Russian crude fell to 1.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in January, their lowest level since November 2022 and down from an average of 1.7 million bpd in 2025. By contrast, Russian crude deliveries to China surged to an all-time high that month.

China faces a tough choice. It must weigh the benefits of cheap Russian crude against steep US trade penalties.

“China systematically opposes extraterritorial jurisdiction, which lacks a basis in international law and does not have the authorisation of the United Nations Security Council,” said the spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Guo Jiakun. Beijing “has always carried out normal economic and trade cooperation with countries around the world on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” he said, adding that “such cooperation is not directed against third parties nor is it subject to interference or coercion by third parties.”

China does have one important advantage over India: Not all of its Russian oil arrives by sea. It receives crude through the Eastern Siberia-Pacific Ocean pipeline system, providing an overland supply route that is unaffected by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

But the calculation for both countries has changed since the war with Iran began. Disruptions to Middle East supplies have made Russian barrels more, rather than less, important to Asian buyers, complicating Washington’s attempt to use access to the US market to pressure Moscow’s largest energy customers.

How will this impact the oil market globally?

The question now is how aggressively Trump will use his new powers, analysts say. The legislation allows him to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent, but does not automatically trigger them.

Trying to squeeze large volumes of Russian crude out of the market, however, could prove particularly difficult at a time when alternate supplies are already under severe pressure.

Iran has de facto controlled traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for joint US-Israeli attacks on its territory since late February, disrupting one of the world’s most important energy routes. About one-fifth of global oil supplies were shipped through the waterway before the war began.

Alternate routes are also under pressure. Following a drone attack last week, Saudi Arabia temporarily shut down its East-West pipeline, the kingdom’s most important route for bypassing Hormuz and transporting crude from its oil-producing east to the Red Sea. Riyadh has already cancelled a number of deliveries to European customers because of the disruption.

If US tariffs push major importers to sharply reduce their purchases of Russian crude as well, they could be forced to compete for barrels elsewhere in an already tight market, potentially sending global oil prices sharply higher.

articles.title: Carmarthenshire businessman Owain Davies killed in Swiss Alps plane crash
articles.summary: Owain Davies’ family said they had “suffered an unimaginable loss”, describing him as “driven and determined”.
articles.body:
A prominent Welsh businessman has been named as one of three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps.

Owain Davies, 55, from west Wales, was managing director of engineering firm Amcanu, based in Burry Port, Carmarthenshire.

His son Aron Davies said the family had "suffered an unimaginable loss", describing his father as "driven, determined and someone who simply didn't accept that a problem was too big to solve".

Davies was killed when the Cirrus SR22T crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday.

Formal identification of the other two victims is under way, including another Briton who is yet to be named.

Authorities said the plane took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, crashed into a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.

Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters.

Amcanu announced his death with "profound sadness", describing Davies as "strong-willed, spirited, determined and deeply caring".

The statement also said family was "at the centre of Owain's life".

"He was devoted to his wife Michelle, immensely proud of his children Aron and Ffion, and adored being a grandfather to Oakley and Albie, " it said.

His son Aron described him as "a real character", and said he was "immensely proud of everything he achieved".

"He was my mentor throughout my life, personally and in business, and I know many people at Amcanu will feel that they have lost a mentor too," he said.

The firm was founded by his father, Spencer Davies OBE, in Burry Port in 1975, and he took over the leadership of the business in 2000.

Amcanu noted Davies was "a proud Welshman and Welsh speaker" and had been a trustee of Wales Air Ambulance Charity since 2017.

Earlier in his life, he served for nearly 25 years as a helmsman with Burry Port Lifeboat, the firm said.

The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation and the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched an inquiry.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland".

It said officials were in contact with the local authorities.

"Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it said.
